lessons.title: Real numbers: rational or irrational
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to classify real numbers as rational or irrational.
lessons.explanation: Rational numbers can be written as a fraction of two integers, with a non-zero denominator. Integers, terminating decimals and recurring decimals are rational. For a non-negative integer radicand, its square root is rational exactly when that integer is a perfect square. More generally, rational radicands can also have rational roots: √(1/4) = 1/2. Numbers such as √2 and π are real but irrational.
lessons.workedExample:
Classify √81.
1. 81 is a non-negative integer and a perfect square: 9 × 9 = 81.
2. √81 = 9.
3. 9 is an integer, so it is rational.
Also, √(1/4) = 1/2, showing that a rational non-integer radicand can have a rational square root.
Therefore √81 is a rational real number.
lessons.misconception: A root sign does not automatically mean “irrational”. For an integer inside √, check whether it is a perfect square; for fractions, simplify the root carefully.

distractorExplanations.B: 0.25 is rational because it equals 1/4. A terminating decimal can be written as a fraction of integers.
distractorExplanations.C: −7 is rational because it equals −7/1. A negative sign does not make a number irrational.
distractorExplanations.D: 3/5 is already a ratio of two integers, so it is rational. An irrational number cannot be expressed in that form.

practiceQuestions.solution: 20 is not a perfect square, so √20 cannot be written as a ratio of integers. The other choices are rational.
practiceQuestions.hint: Check whether the radicand is a perfect square.

feedbackByWrong.−7: −7 is rational because it equals −7/1. A negative sign does not make a number irrational.
feedbackByWrong.3/5: 3/5 is already a ratio of two integers, so it is rational. An irrational number cannot be expressed in that form.

lessons.title: Factors, multiples, HCF and LCM
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to use prime factors to find an HCF or LCM.
lessons.explanation: A factor divides a number exactly; a multiple is made by multiplying. Prime factorisation writes a number as primes. For HCF use only common prime factors at their smallest powers. For LCM use every required prime factor at its largest power.
lessons.workedExample:
Find the HCF and LCM of 24 and 36.
24 = 2³ × 3 and 36 = 2² × 3².
HCF = 2² × 3 = 12.
LCM = 2³ × 3² = 72.
lessons.misconception: Do not choose the HCF when a situation asks when repeated events next happen together: that needs the LCM.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What is the prime factorisation of 84?

distractorExplanations.A: 2 × 3 × 7 equals 42, so one factor of 2 is missing. Divide 84 by 2 twice before using 3 and 7.
distractorExplanations.B: 2³ × 3 × 7 equals 168, so this includes one too many factors of 2. Check that the factors multiply back to 84.
distractorExplanations.C: 2² × 3² × 7 equals 252, so the factor 3 has been used twice. Prime-factor products must equal the original number.

practiceQuestions.hint: Keep dividing by prime numbers.

feedbackByWrong.2² × 3² × 7: 2² × 3² × 7 equals 252, so the factor 3 has been used twice. Prime-factor products must equal the original number.

lessons.title: Ratio and unit rate
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to simplify a ratio and calculate a unit rate.
lessons.explanation: A ratio compares quantities in the same order. Divide every part by the same common factor to simplify it. A rate compares unlike units, for example kilometres per hour. Find a unit rate by dividing to make one of the quantities equal to one.
lessons.workedExample:
A recipe uses 6 cups flour for 4 cups water.
Divide both parts by 2.
6 : 4 = 3 : 2.
For every 3 cups flour, use 2 cups water.
lessons.misconception: Do not add the numbers in a ratio. A ratio is multiplicative: both parts must scale by the same factor.

distractorExplanations.A: 9 : 12 is equivalent to 18 : 24, but it is not fully simplified. Divide both parts by their HCF, 3.
distractorExplanations.B: 42 : 1 changes the relationship rather than simplifying it. A ratio is simplified by dividing every part by the same factor.
distractorExplanations.D: 6 : 8 : 2 has introduced a third part, so it no longer compares the same two quantities. Divide both original parts by 6.

practiceQuestions.solution: The HCF of 18 and 24 is 6. Divide both parts: 18 ÷ 6 : 24 ÷ 6 = 3 : 4.
practiceQuestions.hint: Find a number that divides both parts.

feedbackByWrong.6 : 8 : 2: 6 : 8 : 2 has introduced a third part, so it no longer compares the same two quantities. Divide both original parts by 6.
feedbackByWrong.9 : 12: 9 : 12 is equivalent to 18 : 24, but it is not fully simplified. Divide both parts by their HCF, 3.
feedbackByWrong.42 : 1: 42 : 1 changes the relationship rather than simplifying it. A ratio is simplified by dividing every part by the same factor.

distractorExplanations.C: 47 subtracts the time from the distance. To find a unit rate, divide 150 by 3.

practiceQuestions.solution: Speed = distance ÷ time = 150 ÷ 3 = 50 km/h.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A learner claims that 4 : 6 and 10 : 15 are not equivalent. Which explanation correctly evaluates the claim?

options.A: The claim is incorrect because all ratios are equivalent
options.C: The claim is correct because the numbers in each ratio are different
options.D: The claim is correct because only ratios already in lowest terms can be equivalent

distractorExplanations.A: The claim is incorrect here, but not all ratios are equivalent. Equivalence requires the same simplified ratio, which is 2 : 3.
distractorExplanations.C: Different-looking numbers can name the same ratio. Simplify 4 : 6 and 10 : 15 before comparing their multiplicative relationship.
distractorExplanations.D: A ratio need not already be simplified to be equivalent. Both ratios simplify to 2 : 3.

practiceQuestions.solution: Simplify each ratio by its own common factor: 4 : 6 ÷ 2 = 2 : 3 and 10 : 15 ÷ 5 = 2 : 3. Both describe the same multiplicative relationship, so the learner’s claim is incorrect.
practiceQuestions.hint: Simplify both ratios before deciding.

lessons.title: Direct and inverse proportion
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to decide whether a situation uses direct or inverse proportion.
lessons.explanation: In direct proportion, both quantities change in the same direction at a constant rate: more items cost more. In inverse proportion, one quantity increases while the other decreases so that their product stays fixed: more equally efficient workers take fewer days.
lessons.workedExample:
Four workers take 15 days.
Total work = 4 × 15 = 60 worker-days.
With 6 workers: 60 ÷ 6 = 10 days.
This is inverse proportion.
lessons.misconception: “One goes up and one goes down” is not enough by itself. The total task or product must stay fixed for inverse proportion.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Five notebooks cost R40. What do eight cost at the same price?

distractorExplanations.A: R320 multiplies the total R40 by 8 without first finding one notebook’s price. Use R40 ÷ 5, then multiply by 8.
distractorExplanations.B: R13 is not the cost of eight notebooks at the constant rate. Find the R8 unit price, then scale it to eight.
distractorExplanations.D: R48 uses R6 per notebook, but R40 shared by 5 notebooks is R8 each. Multiply the unit price by 8.

practiceQuestions.solution: One notebook costs R40 ÷ 5 = R8. Eight cost 8 × R8 = R64.
practiceQuestions.hint: Find the cost of one notebook.

feedbackByWrong.R320: R320 multiplies the total R40 by 8 without first finding one notebook’s price. Use R40 ÷ 5, then multiply by 8.
feedbackByWrong.R13: R13 is not the cost of eight notebooks at the constant rate. Find the R8 unit price, then scale it to eight.

lessons.title: Commission, rental and compound interest
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to calculate common Grade 9 financial applications.
lessons.explanation: Commission is a percentage of sales. Rental questions can include a per-day amount, a non-refundable fee, and a refundable deposit; identify which amount is returned before finding the final cost. Compound interest grows the balance each period, so each new percentage is calculated on the previous balance.
lessons.workedExample:
R2 000 earns 10% compound interest for two years.
Year 1: R2 000 × 1.10 = R2 200.
Year 2: R2 200 × 1.10 = R2 420.
The balance is R2 420.
lessons.misconception: Do not add the once-off rental fee once for every day, and do not use simple interest when the question says compound.

distractorExplanations.B: R2 790 is the amount left after subtracting commission, not the commission itself. Calculate 7% of R3 000.
distractorExplanations.C: R700 treats 7% as 7/30 or a much larger percentage. Use 7 ÷ 100 = 0.07, then multiply.

practiceQuestions.hint: Change the percent to a decimal.

lessons.title: Integer operations and order
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to calculate with signed integers using the correct order of operations.
lessons.explanation: For addition and subtraction, use a number line or rewrite subtraction as adding the opposite. lessons.title: Squares, cubes and roots
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to evaluate integer powers and roots.
lessons.explanation: A square multiplies a number by itself; a cube uses three factors. Brackets decide whether a negative sign belongs to the base. √ gives the principal non-negative square root, while cube roots can be negative.
lessons.workedExample:
Evaluate (−4)².
The brackets make −4 the base.
(−4)² = (−4) × (−4) = 16.
lessons.misconception: Without brackets, −4² means −(4²) = −16. The brackets matter.

distractorExplanations.B: −25 keeps a negative sign after squaring. The whole negative number is squared, and two negative factors multiply to a positive.
distractorExplanations.C: −10 doubles −5 instead of squaring it. Squaring means multiplying the base by itself: (−5) × (−5).
distractorExplanations.D: 10 doubles the magnitude rather than squaring. Expand (−5)² as (−5) × (−5) to get a positive product.

practiceQuestions.hint: Square the whole bracketed number.

feedbackByWrong.10: 10 doubles the magnitude rather than squaring. Expand (−5)² as (−5) × (−5) to get a positive product.

feedbackByWrong.−10: −10 doubles −5 instead of squaring it. Squaring means multiplying the base by itself: (−5) × (−5).

distractorExplanations.C: 6 cubed is positive 216, not −216. A cube root of a negative number must be negative.
distractorExplanations.D: −36 is not a cube root; cubing it would be far from −216. Find the number that multiplied by itself three times gives −216.

lessons.title: Exponent laws
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to use product, quotient and power laws for exponents.
lessons.explanation: For the same non-zero base: multiply means add exponents, divide means subtract exponents, and a power of a power means multiply exponents. A quotient law needs a non-zero divisor, for example y⁹ ÷ y⁴ requires y ≠ 0. The base does not change just because the exponent changes.
lessons.workedExample:
Simplify (x³)⁴.
A power of a power multiplies exponents.
(x³)⁴ = x^(3 × 4) = x¹².
lessons.misconception: Do not use the product law for addition: x² + x³ cannot be simplified by adding exponents.

distractorExplanations.B: a¹² multiplies the exponents, which is for a power of a power. With a⁴ × a³, count factors and add exponents.
distractorExplanations.C: a¹ subtracts exponents as if dividing. Multiplication of the same base requires 4 + 3.
distractorExplanations.D: 7a treats exponents as ordinary coefficients. The base stays a and the total number of factors is a⁷.

practiceQuestions.solution: The bases match, so add exponents: 4 + 3 = 7.
practiceQuestions.hint: The base remains a.

feedbackByWrong.a¹: a¹ subtracts exponents as if dividing. Multiplication of the same base requires 4 + 3.
feedbackByWrong.7a: 7a treats exponents as ordinary coefficients. The base stays a and the total number of factors is a⁷.

distractorExplanations.A: 1/y⁵ would be y⁻⁵, not y⁹ ÷ y⁴. Cancel the four denominator factors from the nine numerator factors.
distractorExplanations.C: y¹³ adds exponents as in multiplication. Division of equal non-zero bases cancels four factors, leaving 9 − 4.
distractorExplanations.D: y³⁶ multiplies exponents, which is for a power of a power. Here divide y⁹ by y⁴ and subtract exponents.

practiceQuestions.solution: Because y ≠ 0, the quotient is defined. For division with the same base, subtract: 9 − 4 = 5.
practiceQuestions.hint: Use the quotient law only after checking the divisor is non-zero.

feedbackByWrong.y³⁶: y³⁶ multiplies exponents, which is for a power of a power. Here divide y⁹ by y⁴ and subtract exponents.
feedbackByWrong.1/y⁵: 1/y⁵ would be y⁻⁵, not y⁹ ÷ y⁴. Cancel the four denominator factors from the nine numerator factors.

distractorExplanations.A: n⁹ adds exponents instead of multiplying for a power of a power. Square n³ by using 3 × 2.
distractorExplanations.B: n⁶ is correct, but m² must also be squared. Multiply both inner exponents by the outer 2.
distractorExplanations.D: m⁴ is correct, but n³ squared multiplies 3 by 2, giving n⁶. Apply the outside power to every factor.

practiceQuestions.solution: Apply the outer power to each factor: m^(2×2)n^(3×2).
practiceQuestions.hint: Every exponent inside the bracket is multiplied.

lessons.title: Zero and negative exponents
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to interpret zero and negative exponents.
lessons.explanation: For any non-zero base a, a⁰ = 1. A negative exponent makes a reciprocal: a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ. These follow from the quotient law, for example a³ ÷ a³ = a⁰ = 1.
lessons.misconception: A negative exponent does not make the answer negative. It tells you to use a reciprocal.

distractorExplanations.A: 9⁰ is defined because the base is non-zero. The undefined case to avoid is 0⁰, not 9⁰.
distractorExplanations.C: 0 confuses a zero exponent with a zero base. For non-zero 9, the zero-exponent rule gives 9⁰ = 1.
distractorExplanations.D: 9 keeps the base but ignores the exponent. A non-zero base raised to zero equals 1.

practiceQuestions.solution: Any non-zero number to exponent zero equals 1.
practiceQuestions.hint: The base is non-zero.

feedbackByWrong.0: 0 confuses a zero exponent with a zero base. For non-zero 9, the zero-exponent rule gives 9⁰ = 1.
feedbackByWrong.9: 9 keeps the base but ignores the exponent. A non-zero base raised to zero equals 1.
feedbackByWrong.Undefined: 9⁰ is defined because the base is non-zero. The undefined case to avoid is 0⁰, not 9⁰.

distractorExplanations.A: 100 ignores the negative exponent. A negative exponent means reciprocal, so use 1 divided by 100.
distractorExplanations.B: −0.01 adds a negative sign that is not in the base. The negative exponent changes position, not the sign.
distractorExplanations.D: −100 treats the negative exponent as a negative answer and reverses the reciprocal. First write 10⁻² as 1/10².

practiceQuestions.hint: Write the reciprocal first.

lessons.title: Scientific notation extension
lessons.objective: By the end of this optional extension, you should be able to write large and small numbers in scientific notation.
lessons.explanation: For a positive number, scientific notation writes a number as a × 10ⁿ where 1 ≤ a < 10. For any nonzero real number in standard scientific notation, the coefficient satisfies 1 ≤ |a| < 10, so negative numbers may have a negative coefficient. Moving the decimal left gives a positive exponent; moving it right gives a negative exponent. This optional extension supports number sense but is not a required Term 1 mastery prerequisite.
lessons.workedExample:
Write −4 500 000 in scientific notation.
Keep the sign and move the decimal six places left: −4.5.
Because |−4.5| is between 1 and 10, −4 500 000 = −4.5 × 10⁶ is standard scientific notation.
lessons.misconception: For a nonzero number, the absolute value of the coefficient must be at least 1 but less than 10; 45 × 10⁵ is not standard scientific notation.

distractorExplanations.C: 7.2 is correctly sized, but 10³ moves the decimal only three places to 7 200. Count four places for 72 000.
distractorExplanations.D: 0.72 × 10⁵ has the right value but the coefficient is below 1. Standard notation needs 1 ≤ |a| < 10.

lessons.title: Numeric patterns and differences
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to identify a constant first difference and extend a linear pattern.
lessons.explanation: A linear number pattern has the same change between consecutive terms. This constant first difference is the coefficient of n in its nth-term rule. Use a table to record term number n and value Tn.
lessons.workedExample:
Extend 5, 9, 13, …
First differences: +4, +4.
Add 4 again: 17, then 21.
The pattern has constant first difference 4.
lessons.misconception: Do not use a constant ratio test for a pattern with a constant difference. Ratios are useful for geometric sequences, not these linear patterns.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What is the first difference of 11, 16, 21, 26, …?

distractorExplanations.A: −5 reverses the subtraction order. The pattern increases, so use later term minus earlier term to get +5.
distractorExplanations.C: 11 is the first term, not the difference. Subtract consecutive terms: 16 − 11 and 21 − 16.
distractorExplanations.D: 10 does not match the increase from 11 to 16. Calculate the difference by subtraction, not by combining non-adjacent terms.

practiceQuestions.solution: 16 − 11 = 5, and the same change continues.
practiceQuestions.hint: Subtract consecutive terms.

feedbackByWrong.11: 11 is the first term, not the difference. Subtract consecutive terms: 16 − 11 and 21 − 16.
feedbackByWrong.−5: −5 reverses the subtraction order. The pattern increases, so use later term minus earlier term to get +5.

distractorExplanations.A: 26, 36 changes the step size after the first new term. Add 6 each time to preserve the linear pattern.
distractorExplanations.B: 18, 20 does not continue the +6 difference. Compare 10 − 4 and 16 − 10 before extending.
distractorExplanations.D: 20, 24 uses an increase of 4, but the given terms increase by 6. Continue the same first difference.

lessons.title: Linear nth-term rules
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to find and test a linear nth-term rule.
lessons.explanation: For a linear pattern, start with Tn = dn + c, where d is the first difference. Substitute n = 1 and the first term to find c. Then test the rule with another term; a rule is only useful if it matches the pattern.
lessons.workedExample:
Find the rule for 6, 10, 14, …
Difference d = 4, so Tn = 4n + c.
At n = 1: 4 + c = 6, so c = 2.
Rule: Tn = 4n + 2. Check T2 = 10.

distractorExplanations.C: 3n + 1 gives the wrong constant difference of 3. The sequence rises by 4 each time.
distractorExplanations.D: n + 3 increases by only 1 per term. The coefficient of n must match the first difference, 4.

lessons.title: Geometric matchstick and tile patterns
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to connect a growing diagram to a table and rule.
lessons.explanation: For a visual pattern, count the first few figures carefully and identify what each new figure adds. In a row of joined squares, the first square uses 4 matchsticks and each extra square shares a side, so it adds 3. The rule is M = 3n + 1.
lessons.workedExample:
How many matchsticks for 5 joined squares?
M = 3n + 1.
M = 3(5) + 1 = 16.
So 5 joined squares need 16 matchsticks.
lessons.misconception: Counting 4n treats every square as separate and counts shared sides twice.

practiceQuestions.prompt: How many matchsticks are needed for 4 joined squares in a row?

distractorExplanations.A: 12 uses 3 matchsticks per square but omits the first square’s extra side. A joined row follows 3n + 1.
distractorExplanations.B: 16 counts four sides for every square and double-counts shared sides. Each extra square adds only 3 matchsticks.
distractorExplanations.C: 10 treats the first square as if it also adds only 3 sides. Start with 4, then add 3 for each of the next squares.

practiceQuestions.hint: Each new square adds 3, not 4.
